Community life is richly represented through coverage of weddings, cultural programming, youth activities, and the work of organizations such as the Urban Legaue and YWCA. Collectively, the issue provides a multifacted portrayal of African American civic participation, social life, and political advocacy at a pivotal moment in the early civil rights era.

column35: Contents include but are not limited to African American newspaper featuring extensive coverage of national and local events affecting Black communitites in Iowa and across the United States. It includes reports on Herbert Hoover's presidential victory and its perceived impact on African Americans, congratualtory statements from Black political leaders, and updates on Oscar DePriest's closely won congressional race in Illinois. The paper also highlights community achievement such as the opening of a new Black-owned electric shop, local club gatherings, church events, and progress within the National Benefit Life Insurance Company while also reporting on tragedies, crimes, and legal notices involving Black residents. Additional sections provide health advice, civil rights updates from NAACP branches, preparations for Armistic Day celebrations, and columsn urging political organization and civic participations, offering a board snapshot of Black life, advocacy, and challenges.

Additional sections provide editorials on Black economic self sufficiency, personal announcements, obituraies, local Iowa community news, and advertisements serving Black readers, painting a vivid pciture of African American life and advocacy in the late 1920s

Alongside this major news story, the paper reports on civil rights related legislative debates affecting Black newspapers, community events, church activities, social clubs, sports and national Black advocacy efforts such as calls for government aid to Black workers and sharecroppers. column27: African American Museum of Iowa
column35: The Waterloo Defender, a weekly newspaper for the Black community, was published in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1960s and 1970s. The publication, which covered news of interest to African Americans in Waterloo and beyond, carried the slogan "We will inform the public ... without fear or favor!" Issues in this collection range from 1966 to 1979. The last available issue, dated September 20, 1979, and titled simply The Defender, refers to a gap in coverage in its top story, "Back on the Streets Again." The issues in this collection are digitized versions of microfilm copies; microfilm reels of the Waterloo Defender also contain copies of the 1950s publications The Waterloo Post and The Waterloo Star.

column35: The Waterloo Star was a newspaper for the Black community published weekly in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1950s. It used the same slogan, "Waterloo's Only Negro Newspaper," as an earlier paper, The Waterloo Post. The Star covered news of interest to local African Americans, including racial integration and other political and cultural topics. The issues in this collection range from August to December 1956. They are digitized versions of microfilm copies.

column35: The Weekly Avalanche, a historic Black newspaper, was published in Des Moines beginning in 1891. The publication covered news of interest to African Americans in the state of Iowa. Other issues are not available, and the end date of the publication is unknown. This is a digitized version of a microfilm copy.

column27: African American Museum of Iowa
column35: The first volume and issue of The Iowa Baptist Standard was published on May 21, 1897, in Des Moines. This historic Black newspaper covered news of interest to both secular and Baptist African Americans in the state of Iowa. The front page of the first issue includes an article on why the newspaper was established. Other topics covered in this issue include notable individuals, examples of the "color line" in the United States, and political activity. Later issues are not available, and the end date of the publication is unknown. This is a digitized version of a microfilm copy.

column35: The Waterloo Star was a newspaper for the Black community published weekly in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1950s. It used the same slogan, "Waterloo's Only Negro Newspaper," as an earlier paper, The Waterloo Post. They are digitized versions of microfilm copies.

column27: African American Museum of Iowa
column35: The Waterloo Defender, a weekly newspaper for the Black community, was published in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1960s and 1970s. The publication, which covered news of interest to African Americans in Waterloo and beyond, carried the slogan "We will inform the public ... without fear or favor!" Issues in this collection range from 1966 to 1979. The last available issue, dated September 20, 1979, and titled simply The Defender, refers to a gap in coverage in its top story, "Back on the Streets Again." The issues in this collection are digitized versions of microfilm copies; microfilm reels of the Waterloo Defender also contain copies of the 1950s publications The Waterloo Post and The Waterloo Star.

column27: African American Museum of Iowa
column35: The Waterloo Defender, a weekly newspaper for the Black community, was published in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1960s and 1970s. The publication, which covered news of interest to African Americans in Waterloo and beyond, carried the slogan "We will inform the public ... without fear or favor!" Issues in this collection range from 1966 to 1979. The last available issue, dated September 20, 1979, and titled simply The Defender, refers to a gap in coverage in its top story, "Back on the Streets Again." The issues in this collection are digitized versions of microfilm copies; microfilm reels of the Waterloo Defender also contain copies of the 1950s publications The Waterloo Post and The Waterloo Star.

column27: Iowa State University
column35: The Waterloo Defender, a weekly newspaper for the Black community, was published in Waterloo, Iowa, during the 1960s and 1970s. The publication, which covered news of interest to African Americans in Waterloo and beyond, carried the slogan "We will inform the public ... without fear or favor!" Issues in this collection range from 1966 to 1979. The last available issue, dated September 20, 1979, and titled simply The Defender, refers to a gap in coverage in its top story, "Back on the Streets Again." The issues in this collection are digitized versions of microfilm copies; microfilm reels of the Waterloo Defender also contain copies of the 1950s publications The Waterloo Post and The Waterloo Star.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column27: Des Moines Public Library (Des Moines, Iowa)
column35: Contents include but are not limited to community news, political commentary, church updates, social events, and advertisements centered around African American life in Iowa and surrounding regions during the late 1920s. It reports on political issues such as Herbert Hoover's election, local Republican activities, and the work of Black civic organizations. The paper highlights achievements of Black-owned businesses, church programs, including art exhibits, musical events, and social gatherings, it also contains personal notices like obituaries, illnesses, marriages, and travel updates, alongside legal notices and local incidents such as accidents and crimes. Overall, the document captures a vivid snapshot of Black community life, challenges, accomplishments, and social engagment during that era.

column27: Des Moines Public Library (Des Moines, Iowa)
column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.

column35: Iowa’s Bystander newspaper (going by various titles throughout the years) was established in Des Moines, Iowa in 1894. The weekly newspaper served as the voice of Iowa’s African American community and covered a variety of local, national, and occasionally international matters. Topics focused on the Black community and was founded with this intent. The newspaper went by various titles throughout the years including: Iowa State Bystander, Iowa Bystander, The Bystander, and The New Iowa Bystander.
